Single-Leg BOSU Balance Exercise
The exercise for balancing on a BOSU ball while standing on one leg is known as the single-leg BOSU balance exercise. This exercise is effective for enhancing balance, coordination, and core stability.
Benefits of the Single-Leg BOSU Balance Exercise
• Improves Balance: Standing on one leg challenges your stability.
• Enhances Coordination: Engaging different muscle groups helps improve overall coordination.
• Strengthens Core: The exercise activates core muscles, promoting better posture and stability.
How to Perform the Single-Leg BOSU Balance Exercise
• Positioning: Stand on the dome side of the BOSU ball with one leg.
• Balance: Keep your opposite leg lifted and your core engaged.
• Duration: Aim to hold the position for 10-20 seconds, gradually increasing the time as you improve.
Progression Tips
• Add Movement: Try reaching for objects around you while maintaining balance.
• Close Your Eyes: This increases the challenge by removing visual stability cues.
• Use a Ball: Catch or toss a ball while balancing to further engage your core and coordination.
This exercise is a great way to build foundational balance skills before progressing to more complex movements.

What Are Quad Sets?
Quad sets are a fundamental exercise used in knee rehabilitation. They focus on strengthening the quadriceps muscles located at the front of the thigh. This exercise is particularly beneficial for individuals recovering from knee injuries or surgeries.
How to Perform Quad Sets
Steps to Execute Quad Sets
• Positioning: Sit or lie down with your legs straight.
• Tightening: Tighten the quadriceps muscles while keeping the leg straight. You should see the kneecap move upward.
• Holding: Maintain the contraction for about 5 seconds.
• Releasing: Relax the muscle after the hold.
• Repetitions: Aim for 10 to 15 repetitions, gradually increasing as strength improves.
Tips for Effective Quad Sets
• Ensure no other muscles are contracting to assist the quadriceps.
• Perform the exercise on a flat surface, like a bed or couch, with a towel or pillow under your heel for comfort.
• It is recommended to do these exercises multiple times a day, especially during the early stages of recovery.
Benefits of Quad Sets
• Restores Muscle Function: Helps rebuild strength in the quadriceps.
• Improves Stability: Enhances stability in the knee joint.
• Increases Range of Motion: Aids in regaining mobility after injury or surgery.
Incorporating quad sets into your rehabilitation routine can significantly aid in recovery and improve overall knee function.

Overview of Hip-Out and Hip-In Lateral Steps
Hip-out and hip-in lateral steps are effective exercises designed to strengthen the hip abductors and enhance lateral stability. These movements are beneficial for improving coordination and overall hip function.
Exercise Descriptions
Hip-Out Steps
• Movement: Step out to the side with one leg, keeping the other leg stable.
• Target Muscles: Primarily engages the hip abductors, including the gluteus medius and minimus.
• Benefits: Increases lateral stability and strength in the hip area.
Hip-In Steps
• Movement: Bring the leg back in toward the center after stepping out.
• Target Muscles: Continues to engage the hip abductors while also activating the adductors.
• Benefits: Enhances coordination and control of the hip joint.
Key Benefits of Lateral Steps
| Benefit | Description |
|---|---|
| Strengthening Hip Abductors | Improves muscle strength around the hip joint. |
| Enhancing Stability | Increases lateral stability, reducing the risk of falls. |
| Improving Coordination | Develops better control and movement patterns in the hips. |
Incorporating hip-out and hip-in lateral steps into a regular exercise routine can lead to improved hip strength and stability, which is essential for various physical activities and daily movements.

Single-Leg Soft-Landing Holds
Single-leg soft-landing holds are exercises that focus on balance and stability by landing softly on one leg and holding the position. This exercise helps improve proprioception and can be beneficial for rehabilitation and athletic training.
Overview
Single-leg soft-landing holds are exercises designed to enhance balance, stability, and proprioception. They involve landing softly on one leg and maintaining that position for a brief period. This exercise is particularly useful in rehabilitation settings and for athletes looking to improve their performance.
Benefits
• Improves balance: Enhances stability by training the body to control weight distribution on one leg.
• Enhances proprioception: Increases awareness of body position, which is crucial for injury prevention.
• Supports rehabilitation: Helps individuals recover from lower-limb injuries by strengthening muscles and improving joint stability.
How to Perform Single-Leg Soft-Landing Holds
Steps
• Preparation: Stand on a stable surface or a box.
• Takeoff: Step off the box or surface with one leg, ensuring that you do not jump.
• Landing: Land softly on the target leg, allowing the knee and hip to bend slightly.
• Hold position: Maintain balance in the landed position for up to 2 seconds.
• Reset: Return to the starting position and repeat.
Key Points to Remember
• Keep your chest up and engage your core for better stability.
• Ensure your knee aligns with the midline of your foot during landing.
• Focus on a controlled descent to minimize impact.
Conclusion
Incorporating single-leg soft-landing holds into your training routine can significantly enhance your balance and stability, making it a valuable exercise for both rehabilitation and athletic performance.

Set a cable pulley at the lowest position and attach a single handle. Stand side-on to the machine, hold the frame with your near hand and lean your body away so you hang at an angle. With the far hand, grasp the handle in front of your hips and raise your arm out to the side to shoulder height with a slight bend in the elbow. Lower slowly. The lean increases tension on the side delts at the bottom of the movement. Complete all reps, then switch sides.

Adjust the seat so that your armpits rest on the top edge of the pad and your upper arms lie flat on it. Grip the handles with your palms facing up.
Curl the handles up by bending your elbows, without lifting your upper arms off the pad or leaning back. Squeeze the biceps briefly at the top, then lower the handles slowly until your arms are almost straight.

Sit on the floor with your legs straight out in front of you and your back tall. Loop a resistance band around the soles of both feet and hold one end in each hand, arms extended and a slight bend in the knees. Pull the band toward your lower ribs by driving your elbows straight back and squeezing your shoulder blades together. Keep your chest up and your torso still rather than rocking backward to move the band. Extend the arms slowly to return. Because the torso stays upright and supported, this is a useful row when a bent-over position is uncomfortable, and it needs no anchor point.

Performed with a flexible resistance bar such as a Theraband FlexBar. Rest your forearm on your thigh or a table with the palm facing down and the wrist just past the edge. Hold the bar in that hand, let the wrist drop, then extend the wrist to raise the bar, keeping the forearm still. Lower slowly, taking about three seconds. The resistance comes from twisting or bending the flexible bar, so a thicker or stiffer bar increases the load. Commonly used for wrist and forearm strengthening and for elbow tendon rehabilitation.

Performed with a flexible resistance bar such as a Theraband FlexBar. Rest your forearm on your thigh or a table with the palm facing up and the wrist just past the edge. Hold the bar in that hand, let the wrist extend back, then curl the wrist up to raise the bar while the forearm stays still. Lower slowly, taking about three seconds. Works the wrist flexors, and is the companion movement to FlexBar wrist extension for balanced forearm strengthening.

An eccentric exercise for the wrist extensors, done with a flexible resistance bar such as a Theraband FlexBar, and widely used in rehabilitation for lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow). Hold the bar vertically in the affected hand with the wrist extended. Grasp the top of the bar with the other hand, palm facing away, and twist the top hand to wind up the bar. Bring both arms out in front of you with the bar horizontal, then slowly let the affected wrist untwist the bar over about four seconds while the other hand holds steady. Reset and repeat. The reverse version, twisting in the opposite direction for the wrist flexors, is used for medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow). Move slowly and stop if the exercise causes sharp pain rather than the expected mild discomfort.

Lie on your back with your knees bent, or sit comfortably. Breathe in slowly into your belly and let your pelvic floor relax and gently lengthen downwards, without pushing or straining. Breathe out and let the pelvic floor return to its resting position. Repeat slowly for several breaths.
The reverse Kegel trains relaxing the pelvic floor, the opposite of the contraction in a regular Kegel exercise.

Lie on your back and pull your knees towards your armpits. Hold the outside of your feet, your ankles or your shins, with the soles of your feet facing the ceiling and your shins roughly vertical.
Gently pull your feet down to open the hips while keeping your lower back and head on the floor. Hold the position and breathe calmly, you can also rock gently from side to side.

Stand upright with a dumbbell in each hand, arms hanging at your sides and feet hip-width apart. For a larger range of motion, stand with the balls of your feet on a step or a weight plate.
Rise up onto your toes as high as you can and pause briefly at the top. Then lower your heels slowly until you feel a stretch in your calves. Keep your knees straight but not locked and your upper body upright.
Use the same technic as your normal squat. Except that you make a pause at the bottom of the squat for about 1-2 seconds, in other words a bit longer than your normal squat.

Go into a one-legged kneeling position and grab the cable from the lowest position.
Rotate the upper torso to get into the starting position and bend the upper torso a little bit sidewise.
Place the unused hand on the knee.
Pull the cable while rotating the upper torso.

A gentle stretch to restore full knee extension. Sit with one leg stretched out in front of you and the heel propped on the floor or a low surface, so the knee is unsupported. Place both hands on the thigh just above the kneecap. Keeping the leg relaxed, gently press down through the hands toward the floor until you feel a stretch behind the knee, and hold for about three seconds before releasing. The pressure should produce a stretch, never sharp pain. Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions, then switch legs.

A banded walking drill for the glutes and hip stabilisers. Place a mini band around both thighs just above the knees, or around the ankles for a harder version. Stand with feet hip-width apart so the band is under tension, then sink into a quarter-squat with the chest up. Walk forward with small diagonal steps, pushing each leg out against the band and keeping the knees tracking over the toes rather than letting them fall inward. Walk forward for the prescribed number of steps, then walk backward to return, keeping the band under tension throughout.

Stand on a step or a sturdy raised surface with the balls of both feet on the edge and the heels hanging off, holding a rail or wall for balance. Let one or both heels drop below the level of the step until you feel a stretch through the calf, and hold. Keep the knee straight to stretch the gastrocnemius, or bend the knee slightly to bias the soleus lower down. Hold for the prescribed time, typically 30 seconds, without bouncing, then switch sides if stretching one leg at a time.

A balance and proprioception drill. Stand on one leg with the knee slightly bent and the other foot lifted clear of the floor, then close your eyes and hold the position. Without visual feedback the ankle and hip stabilisers have to do the work, so expect noticeable wobble. Stand within reach of a wall, counter or chair so you can steady yourself if needed. Hold for the prescribed time, then switch legs. Commonly prescribed in rehabilitation after ankle or knee injury.

A balance drill that adds a moving load. Stand on one leg with the knee slightly bent, holding a kettlebell in one hand. Pass the kettlebell around your body in a circle, handing it from one hand to the other in front and behind you, while keeping your balance on the standing leg. Keep the hips level and the torso upright; the shifting weight of the bell constantly changes your centre of mass, which is what trains the hip and ankle stabilisers. Complete the prescribed number of circles, reverse direction, then switch legs. Use a light bell to start.

How to Perform It
• Hold a dumbbell in each hand with a neutral or overhand grip.
• Hinge at the hips, pushing your glutes back, until your torso is roughly 45–75 degrees to the floor. Keep a slight bend in your knees.
• Let the dumbbells hang directly below your shoulders with arms fully extended.
• Keep your back flat, chest up, and core braced — avoid rounding your spine.
• Pull the dumbbells up toward your ribcage/hips, driving your elbows back and squeezing your shoulder blades together at the top.
• Pause briefly at the top of the movement.
• Lower the dumbbells back down under control to the starting position.
• Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
Key Coaching Cues
• Hinge from the hips, not the lower back
• Keep the spine neutral throughout — no rounding
• Lead with the elbows, not the hands
• Avoid using momentum or jerking the weight up
• Control the eccentric (lowering) phase rather than letting the weights drop

Full-body mobility and dynamic warm-up routine (3–5 minutes) to prepare joints, muscles, and the cardiovascular system for workout.
Movement Flow:
Deep Breathing & Arm Raises: Inhale while raising arms laterally overhead, exhale as you lower them.
Knee Bends: Soft, rhythmic knee flexions synchronized with arm swings.
Arm Circles: Large full-range arm rotations forward, then backward to open up the chest and shoulder girdle.
Chest Expansion: Cross arms in front of the chest and open wide to the sides.
Side Bends: Reach overhead to stretch the lateral torso left and right with a smooth side flexion.
Forward & Back Bends: Gently hinge at the hips to reach forward, then return upright with a mild spinal extension.
Torso Twists: Swing arms side-to-side to rotate the spine and loosen the core.
Ankle Mobility / Light Bounces: Soft heel lifts or light bouncing on toes to warm up lower leg joints and tendons.

Kelso shrugs are a variation of scapular shrugs designed primarily to train scapular retraction, with particular emphasis on the middle trapezius, rhomboids, and, secondarily, the lower trapezius. Unlike conventional shrugs, the goal is not to elevate the shoulders toward the ears, but rather to pull the shoulder blades backward.
They are typically performed with the chest supported on an incline bench, using either dumbbells or a barbell:
• Lie face down on an incline bench, with your arms extended toward the floor.
• Keep your elbows almost completely locked throughout the movement.
• Starting with the shoulder blades slightly protracted, retract them, trying to bring them closer together.
• Keep your chest firmly supported on the bench; avoid turning the movement into a row by extending your torso.
• Briefly hold the fully retracted position, then return in a controlled manner, allowing the shoulder blades to separate.

• Starting position: Lie flat on your back with knees bent, feet flat on the floor (or stand/sit upright).
• Exhalation: Fully exhale all the air from your lungs through your mouth.
• Contraction: Draw your navel in towards your spine as far as possible, pulling your stomach inward and up under your ribcage.
• Hold: Hold this isometric contraction without breathing for 10 to 20 seconds.
• Release: Slowly inhale through your nose to release the tension and relax your abdominals.
• Repeat: Rest briefly and perform the desired number of sets.

Starting position
Step into the captain's chair (vertical knee raise station). Rest your forearms on the pads and hold the handles. Keep your upper body upright, look straight ahead and press your back against the pad, without rounding or arching it. Your legs are almost straight with a slight bend in the knees, your feet are off the floor and your legs are together.
Movement
Pull your bent legs up, bringing your knees towards your chest. Only go as high as you can while keeping good form, with your legs together the whole time. Then lower your legs again while inhaling, without putting your feet back on the floor.

Starting position
Step into the captain's chair (dip station). Rest your forearms on the pads and grip the handles firmly. Keep your back upright and close to the pad and look straight ahead. Bend your legs so that your thighs and shins form roughly a right angle.
Movement
Raise your knees while turning your legs slightly to one side, about 30-45 degrees, keeping your thighs parallel to the floor. Then do the same to the other side. You can pause briefly in the middle or go straight to the other side.

Weighted neck flexion is an isolation exercise designed to strengthen the anterior (front) neck flexor muscles by bringing your chin toward your chest against external resistance (most commonly a light weight plate, resistance band, or neck harness).

Strength training exercise where you push a weight away from your body using one leg at a time on a leg press machine. It helps to improve leg strength, balance, and muscular symmetry by isolating each leg individually. This exercise is particularly useful for identifying and correcting muscle imbalances between your legs.
Perform a row using gymnastic rings, but with the body position somewhere between vertical and horizontal. Go closer to horizontal to make it harder.

Starting Position
• Feet: Place the soles of your feet flat against a vertical wall, with your toes or balls of your feet on the floor.
• Hands: Position your hands on the floor shoulder-width apart, directly under your lower chest or solar plexus.
• Body: Keep your core tight, glutes squeezed, and head in a neutral position. Your knees should hover a few inches above the floor without touching it.
Movement Pattern
• Lower Down: Flex your elbows (tucked around 45 degrees) to lower your chest toward the floor, stopping just a few centimeters short of touching the ground.
• Rock Back: As you press upward through your arms, push your hips backward and bend your knees, rocking your weight toward your heels while keeping your shins nearly parallel to the floor.
• Drive Forward: Explode forward from your lower-body/crouched position, shifting your weight back into the starting push-up plank stance to complete the repetition.
Key Tips for Proper Form
• Keep Knees Low: Do not let your knees or hips pike high up in the air; keep the motion low and horizontal.
• Maintain Wall Contact: Keep the soles of your feet pressed against the wall so you don't lose your leverage.
• Engage the Core: Avoid arching your lower back by tilting your pelvis backward and bracing your abs.

Start on all fours with your palms flat on the floor. Slowly rock forward and backward, keeping your hands planted. Move only within a comfortable, pain-free wrist range to gently improve mobility and flexibility.

Start in a straight-arm plank with your hands under your shoulders. Keep your elbows locked and move only your shoulder blades: let your chest sink slightly, then push the floor away to spread the shoulder blades. Move in a comfortable, controlled range.
Dumbbell squats with elevated heel position. Stand on either squat wedges or weight plates to raise heels higher than toes, while holding the dumbbells on your sides.

Push ups for targeting triceps.
• Start with a plank position with your hands directly below your shoulders, feet together.
• When descending, keep your elbows pinned to your sides. Upper arms straight back.
• Lower until your chest touches the floor, then return.

Extend your right arm straight across your chest toward the left. Hook your left arm around your right elbow and pull your right arm a little closer to your body. Keep your shoulder down as you do this. Repeat on the other side.

Extend your right arm straight out in front of you, with your palm facing up (fingers pointing toward the floor). Using your left hand, gently pull the fingers of your right hand toward you until you feel a stretch in your forearm and biceps.

Stand on one leg (hold onto a wall if necessary). Use your hand to grasp the ankle of your other leg and gently pull your heel toward your buttocks. Make sure your knees stay close together and that you push your pelvis slightly forward (avoid arching your back).

One of the best exercises for the rectus abdominis muscles. Lie on your back with your legs straight and your arms close to your sides. Lift your head off the floor and raise your legs and arms about 15 centimeters off the floor. Your palms should face down, and look up at the ceiling.
Now bend your legs and at the same time sit up so that your knees and chest almost touch. Only your buttocks are still on the floor. Your arms are now extended at shoulder height. Then slowly return to the starting position with your arms and legs extended and your head raised.

A static hold from a pull-up bar with straight elbows and actively depressed, stabilized shoulders. Grip a secure bar and let your body hang under control. Keep your elbows straight and gently draw your shoulders down, away from your ears. Maintain this active shoulder position without pulling up, swinging, or repeatedly moving the shoulder blades. Hold for up to 30 seconds. Stop earlier if your grip opens, shoulder control deteriorates, or pain occurs. Record actual seconds, grip, and any assistance used. This is distinct from a relaxed passive dead hang or a moving scapular pull-up.

A static bodyweight support with both hands and feet on the floor and hips raised in a pike position. Place your hands and feet securely on the floor, then raise your hips. Keep your elbows straight and actively push the floor away through your shoulders. Maintain a controlled, stationary position without bending your elbows, lowering your head for push-up repetitions, or raising your feet onto a surface. Hold for up to 30 seconds. Stop earlier for loss of alignment, loss of active shoulder support, or pain. Record actual seconds, hand and foot spacing, and alignment. This is the floor variation, not a pike push-up or an elevated-feet pike hold.

Swim one short pool length at a gentle pace while focusing on a relaxed body position and a steady exhale into the water between breaths. Pause at the wall between lengths. This is a moving swim technique drill, not stationary bobbing or a kickboard-only exercise.

Place both hands against a wall above shoulder height. Step back and gently move the chest downward while reaching the arms overhead, keeping the back controlled. Hold a comfortable shoulder flexion stretch without forcing the range or arching the lower back.

Hold a stable straight bar in front of the hips with both arms straight. Keep both feet on the floor or a stable platform so they assist your body weight. Maintain steady shoulders and a controlled supported position without swinging. This is a feet-assisted straight-bar support hold, not a ring hold or a full dip.

Swim a short pool length at a controlled brisk effort, maintaining smooth strokes and steady breathing. Stop at the wall for the prescribed recovery before the next repeat. This is a submaximal swim interval, not an all-out sprint; distance, repeats and rest are set by the routine.

Hold a stable support in front of you and lower into a comfortable deep squat with both feet grounded. Use the support for balance and to control depth. Maintain the squat hold without bouncing or forcing the hips or ankles farther than a comfortable range.

Stand tall with your arm hanging straight down by your side. Hold a dumbbell by one end of the handle so the weighted end points forward and your thumb is on top. Keep the arm completely still and tip the weighted end up toward the ceiling using only the wrist, then lower it slowly. This trains radial deviation, the riser used in arm wrestling. Slide your hand further from the weight to make it harder.

Set up exactly as for dumbbell wrist rising: arm straight down by your side, dumbbell held at one end with the weight pointing forward. Tip the weight up to the top position and hold it still for the set time without letting it drop. This builds tendon strength in the riser for arm wrestling. Start light and stop if you feel sharp pain in the wrist or elbow.

Rest your forearm on a bench or your knee and hold a light kettlebell by the handle with the bell hanging down. Keeping the elbow and forearm still, slowly rotate your wrist so the palm turns down, then rotate back so the palm turns up. Do the set number of turns in each direction. This trains pronation and supination for grip and arm wrestling.

Rest your forearm on a bench with the palm facing in and the thumb on top. Hold a dumbbell by one end with the weighted end pointing up. Let the weight tip about 45 degrees toward the palm up side, then stop it and hold that position for the set time. The muscles that stop it falling are your pronators, which roll the hand over in arm wrestling. Start with a light weight because the leverage is high.

Sit on a bench with your forearm resting on your thigh, palm facing up, holding a dumbbell or barbell. Curl the wrist all the way up and hold the top position for the set time, squeezing hard. This builds cupping strength and tendon resilience for grip and arm wrestling. Do it straight after your wrist curls without changing seats.

Stand on a box or bench under a pull-up bar and step up so your chin is above the bar with your elbows fully bent. Take your feet off the box and lower yourself as slowly as you can, aiming for five seconds, until your arms are straight. Step back onto the box and repeat. This builds the strength needed for full pull-ups.

Use a box or bench to get your chin above a pull-up bar with your elbows fully bent and shoulders pulled down. Take your feet off the box and hold that top position still for the set time. Keep your chest up and do not let your chin drop below the bar. This strengthens the hardest part of the pull-up.

Hang two towels over a pull-up bar, one for each hand. Grip a towel tightly in each hand and hang with your arms straight and your shoulders active for as long as you can. The thick, unstable towels make your grip work much harder than a normal bar. This builds crushing grip strength for arm wrestling.

Attach a single handle to a low cable. Rest your forearm on a bench or your thigh with the palm facing up and the cable pulling your hand away from you. Curl your fingers and wrist toward you as if cupping a ball, squeeze for a second, then lower slowly. This builds the wrist flexion used to control an opponent's hand in arm wrestling.

Set a cable at chest height and stand side on, holding the handle with your elbow bent about ninety degrees in front of you, like an arm wrestling setup. Pull the handle toward your body using your biceps and back, keeping the wrist cupped, then return slowly. This trains the hook or back pressure used in arm wrestling.

Set a cable at chest height and stand side on with the cable on your working side. Hold the handle with your elbow bent about ninety degrees and close to your body. Press the handle across your body toward your opposite side using your chest and shoulder, then return slowly. This trains the side pressure used to pin an opponent in arm wrestling.

Attach a strap or handle to a cable at hand height so the cable pulls your palm toward facing up. Keep your elbow bent at your side and still. Rotate your forearm so the palm turns down against the cable, then let it rotate back slowly. This builds pronation strength for rolling an opponent's hand in arm wrestling.

Attach a strap or handle to a cable at hand height so the cable pulls your palm toward facing down. Keep your elbow bent at your side and still. Rotate your forearm so the palm turns up against the cable, then let it rotate back slowly. This balances pronation work and protects the elbow.

Hold a sledgehammer or an empty dumbbell handle with a plate on one end near the bottom of the handle, arm by your side. Using only the wrist, lift the head up in front of you, then lower it slowly. Turn around so the head is behind you to train the opposite direction. Move your hand further from the weight to make it harder.

Stand with your arm straight down by your side. Hold a dumbbell by one end of the handle with the weighted end pointing behind you. Keeping the arm still, lift the weighted end up behind you using only the wrist, then lower it slowly. This is the opposite of wrist rising and keeps the wrist balanced.

Hold a wrist roller, a short bar with a rope and a small weight attached, with both hands at shoulder height and arms straight out in front. Roll the bar with your wrists to wind the rope up until the weight reaches the bar, then unwind it slowly. Roll forward and backward on different sets to train both sides of the forearm.

Hold a spring hand gripper deep in your palm. Squeeze until the handles touch, hold for a second, then open slowly. Use a gripper strength you can close for the target reps. This builds crushing grip strength for holding on in arm wrestling and in pulling exercises.

Put a small rubber band around all five fingertips. Spread your fingers and thumb open as wide as possible against the band, hold for a second, then close slowly. This trains the extensor muscles that open the hand and balances heavy gripping, which helps keep the elbows and wrists healthy.

Place a weight plate on the floor with the hub facing up, or use a loading pin with a plate attached. Pinch the hub with your fingertips on one side and your thumb on the other, then stand up and hold it for the set time. This builds thumb and pinch strength, which helps grip control in arm wrestling.

Fit thick grip sleeves over two dumbbell handles, or wrap the handles in a towel to make them thicker. Stand tall holding one in each hand at your sides and hold for the set time without letting the handles roll in your hands. The thicker handle makes your fingers and thumb work much harder than a normal grip.

Fill a deep bucket with dry rice. Push your hand into the rice and repeatedly open and close your fist, twist your wrist both ways, and spread your fingers against the rice for the set time. This is a low impact way to train every muscle of the hand and forearm and is good for warming up or recovery.

Hang two towels over a pull-up bar and grip one in each hand. Pull yourself up until your hands are near your chin, then lower slowly to straight arms. Holding the towels makes your grip work much harder than a normal pull-up. Use assistance or do negatives if you cannot do full reps yet.

Grip a hanging climbing rope with both hands overhead. Pull yourself up hand over hand, using your legs to clamp the rope if needed, then climb down with control. Beginners can start seated on the floor and pull up to standing. This builds pulling and grip strength together.

Stand under a pull-up bar on the floor or a low box so you can reach the bar with bent arms. Jump and pull at the same time until your chin passes the bar, then lower yourself as slowly as you can. This is a beginner step toward full pull-ups.
Perform the leg press with controlled form, feet shoulder-width on the platform, lower slowly without letting the pelvis lift, keep knees tracking over toes, breathe steadily.
Perform the Bulgarian split squat with an upright torso, rear foot on a bench, lower until the front thigh is parallel, keep the knee over the toes, hold a rack for balance if needed.
Perform the hip thrust with shoulder blades on the bench, drive through the heels, squeeze the glutes at the top for one second, avoid overextending the lower back, lower slowly.
Lie on your back, press your lower back into the floor, extend opposite arm and leg slowly, keep the spine neutral, breathe steadily, return under control without arching.
On all fours, extend opposite arm and leg, keep the pelvis level and the spine neutral, move slowly under control, return to the start without letting the lower back sag.
Hold a side plank on your elbow, keep pelvis, ribcage and spine aligned in one straight line, breathe normally, avoid sagging the hips or shrugging the shoulder.
Sit with your back supported, keep the upper arms fixed at your sides, curl the dumbbells up, pause briefly at the top, lower slowly under control without swinging the back.

Lie on your back, breathe in fully, let the ribs sink down, press the lower back into the floor, exhale slowly while keeping intra-abdominal pressure, five reps per set.

Lie on your back with both legs extended. Raise one leg straight up and gently pull it towards your upper body with both hands around your thigh. Keep the knee as straight as possible and your lower back on the mat. Hold the stretch, then switch legs.
